events.label: Stone pillars at Göbekli Tepe

place.name: Göbekli Tepe, near Şanlıurfa, southeast Turkey (37.22 N, 38.92 E)

events.summary: About 9500 BCE. On a hill in what is now southeast Turkey, people who hunted and gathered their food carved stone pillars as tall as a house and stood them in rings. Nobody knows why.

paragraphs: A stone pillar stands in a ring of other pillars. It is shaped like a capital T, is as tall as a two-storey house, and weighs about as much as seven cars. Down its sides, someone carved two long arms. The hands meet at the front, above a belt. Other pillars nearby are covered with carved foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and scorpions.
The hill is called Göbekli Tepe, which means "Potbelly Hill" in Turkish. Say "guh-bek-LEE TEP-eh." It is in southeast Turkey.
The pillars were cut from the limestone of the hill itself with flint tools.
One pillar was never finished. It still lies where it was being cut, seven metres long. Standing, it would have weighed about fifty tonnes.
What makes the pillars strange is that no one knows much about the people who made them. At that time, nobody in the world farmed. Nobody kept sheep.
Still, moving one of these stones could have taken hundreds of people pulling together. It must have taken months or years to build. All of those people had to be fed while they worked.
So what did the builders eat?

They hunted gazelle and gathered wild plants, including wild wheat. Within about a thousand years, and not far away, people were farming wheat. But so far as we know, there were no farms when this was being built.

Nobody knows what the rings were for, either. Klaus Schmidt thought the rings were a temple, a place people travelled to but did not live. He was the archaeologist who began digging at the site in 1995 and realised its importance.

Newer digging has found tanks cut into the rock to hold rainwater, and a great many stones for grinding seeds. Those suggest people lived there too. Even now, most of the hill has not been explored. There is much more to be discovered.
For now, we know the pillars with arms have no faces. Maybe someday we'll know why.

events.label: Maize

place.name: the Balsas River valley, Guerrero, southwest Mexico (18.3 N, 99.8 W). The exact spot is unknown.

events.summary: About 7000 BCE. In the hills of southwest Mexico, people began choosing seeds from a wild grass called teosinte. Over thousands of years it became maize, the corn that now feeds much of the world.

paragraphs: A wild grass grows on the hillsides of southwest Mexico. Its name is teosinte. Say "tay-oh-SIN-tay." Its ear is about as long as your little finger, and it holds only five to twelve seeds. Each seed is locked inside a case so hard that you could break a tooth on it.
This grass is the ancestor of corn.
How do you get from one to the other?

Someone had to choose. Every year, the people who gathered teosinte kept some seeds to plant. If they kept seeds from the plants they liked best, with bigger ears or softer cases, the next year's plants were a little more like that. Nobody planned corn. It happened a little at a time, over thousands of years, because people kept choosing.

We know roughly where it started because of the plant's own genes. Every kind of maize in the world is most closely related to the teosinte that grows in the Balsas River valley. In a rock shelter there, archaeologists found grinding stones with tiny grains of maize starch still stuck to them. The grains are about 8,700 years old.
The earliest maize cobs that survive, from a dry cave in Oaxaca, are about 6,250 years old. They are about as long as the top joint of your thumb.
A scientist named George Beadle once heated teosinte seeds in a pan. They popped. So one of the first things people could have done with teosinte, even before it changed, was make popcorn.
Today more maize is grown than any other grain.
Teosinte still grows wild in those hills. It still has its hard little seeds.

events.picturesWanted: a teosinte ear beside a modern corn cob, at the same scale (widely photographed; a public-domain or CC version is needed).
references: Dolores Piperno and others, "Starch grain and phytolith evidence for early ninth millennium B.P. maize from the Central Balsas River Valley, Mexico," *PNAS*, 2009. The grinding stones and the 8,700-year date.
Dolores Piperno and Kent Flannery, "The earliest archaeological maize from highland Mexico," *PNAS*, 2001. The Guilá Naquitz cobs.
Yoshihiro Matsuoka and others, "A single domestication for maize shown by multilocus microsatellite genotyping," *PNAS*, 2002. All maize descends from Balsas teosinte.
John Doebley, "The genetics of maize evolution," *Annual Review of Genetics*, 2004. Teosinte's ear and hard case.

events.label: Storegga slide

place.name: the Storegga, on the edge of the sea floor off western Norway (64.5 N, 5.5 E)

events.summary: About 6150 BCE. Under the sea off Norway, a piece of the sea floor almost as big as Iceland slid into deep water. The tsunami it made swept across the North Sea to Scotland and beyond.

paragraphs: In the Shetland Islands, north of Scotland, there is a layer of sand in the peat. The peat was made by plants, slowly, in quiet water. The sand does not belong there. It was thrown in by the sea, and in some places it lies about twenty metres above where the sea was at the time.
Something threw the sea that high.

Off the coast of Norway, the sea floor ends at a steep edge. Beyond it the water is thousands of metres deep. About 8,200 years ago, a piece of that edge broke loose and slid down into the deep. It covered an area almost as big as Iceland. The mud and sand that moved would bury the whole of Scotland about forty metres deep.

When that much sea floor moves at once, the water above it moves too. That is a tsunami: a wave caused not by wind but by the ground under the sea. The wave spread across the North Sea in a few hours. Its sand is found in Norway, Scotland, the Faroe Islands and Shetland.
Where the North Sea is now, there was land.

The ice had melted, and the sea was rising, but slowly. Between Britain and the rest of Europe lay low hills, marshes and rivers, where people hunted and fished. Archaeologists call it Doggerland. By the time of the slide much of it was already underwater, and what was left may have been islands.
Did the wave finish Doggerland? Some scientists think it did. Others think the islands lasted a while longer. Nobody knows how many people lived there, or how many were lost.
Fishing boats still pull up bones and stone tools from the bottom of the North Sea.

events.picturesWanted: a map of the North Sea with Doggerland's coast about 8,000 years ago (several published reconstructions; licence to check); the Colinda harpoon point, trawled up in 1931 (British Museum or Norwich Castle).
references: Petter Bryn and others, "Explaining the Storegga Slide," *Marine and Petroleum Geology*, 2005. Size and cause of the slide.
Stein Bondevik and others, "Record-breaking height for 8000-year-old tsunami in the North Atlantic," *Eos*, 2003. The Shetland deposits.

events.label: Writing at Uruk

place.name: Uruk (now Warka), southern Iraq (31.32 N, 45.64 E)

events.summary: About 3300 BCE. In Uruk, in what is now Iraq, people began pressing signs into wet clay to keep track of barley, beer and sheep. It is one of the two oldest kinds of writing we know of.

paragraphs: A piece of clay about the size of a bar of soap has marks pressed into it. Some of the marks are round holes. Some are little wedges. One looks like a jar with a pointed bottom.
The round holes and wedges are numbers. The jar means beer.

This is some of the oldest writing in the world. It was found in the ruins of Uruk, a city in what is now southern Iraq, which about 5,300 years ago was one of the largest cities anywhere. Archaeologists have dug up about five thousand tablets like it there.
What did the first writers write about?

Mostly, things to count. How much barley came in. How much went out. How many sheep, how much beer, how many workers and how much each was paid. Almost every early tablet is a record of this kind. A few are lists of words, which may have been how the writers learned the signs.

The writer held a sharpened reed and pressed it into clay while the clay was still soft. Then the tablet dried hard. A dried tablet lasts a very long time, and if a building burns down around it, it bakes and lasts even longer.

Some tablets end with a sign that may be a person's name: Kushim. It appears on several records of barley. If it is a name, Kushim is one of the first people in history whose name we can read, and what we know about Kushim is that he or she was keeping accounts. But the sign may be a title instead of a name. Nobody is sure.
Over the next thousand years, the signs became wedge-shaped marks called cuneiform. Say "kyoo-NAY-i-form." People used them to write laws, letters, stories and poems.
It started with beer and barley.

references: Hans Nissen, Peter Damerow and Robert Englund, *Archaic Bookkeeping: Early Writing and Techniques of Economic Administration in the Ancient Near East* (University of Chicago Press, 1993). What the early tablets record.
Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (cdli.earth). Images and readings of Uruk tablets, including those naming Kushim.
Irving Finkel and Jonathan Taylor, *Cuneiform* (British Museum Press, 2015). How cuneiform grew from these signs.

events.label: Ötzi, the man in the ice

place.name: the Tisenjoch pass, Ötztal Alps, on the border of Italy and Austria (46.78 N, 10.84 E)

events.summary: About 3300 BCE. A man died high in the Alps between what are now Italy and Austria. The ice kept his body, clothes and tools until two hikers found him in 1991.

paragraphs: In September 1991, two hikers crossing a pass high in the Alps saw a brown shape sticking out of melting ice. It was a man's head and shoulders. They thought he was a climber who had died a few years before.
He had died about 5,300 years before.
He is called Ötzi, after the Ötztal, the valley below. Say "UHT-see." The ice had kept not only his body but everything he carried. Nothing else like it has ever been found from that time.
What did a man carry, 5,300 years ago, on a walk through the mountains?

An axe with a blade of almost pure copper. A bow of yew wood, taller than he was, not yet finished. A quiver holding fourteen arrows, only two of them ready to shoot. A flint knife. A fur hat. Shoes with bearskin soles, stuffed with grass to keep his feet warm. A pouch with a fire-making kit.
Scientists could even tell what he last ate. His stomach held ibex meat and bread made from an early kind of wheat.
He was about forty-five years old. His skin carries sixty-one tattoos, made of short lines rubbed with charcoal. Most are on his back and legs, over places where his joints would have ached.

For ten years, everyone thought he had died of cold. Then, in 2001, an X-ray showed a stone arrowhead in his left shoulder. Someone had shot him from behind. He probably died soon after. Nobody knows who shot him, or why.
Ötzi is now in a museum in Bolzano, Italy. He is kept in a cold room, as cold as the glacier was, and visitors can look at him through a small window.

events.picturesWanted: the copper axe; the reconstructed shoe (South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, which licenses images).
references: South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, "Ötzi – the Iceman" (iceman.it). Finds, the cold room, the museum's own summary.

events.label: Drains of Mohenjo-daro

place.name: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh, Pakistan (27.33 N, 68.14 E)

events.summary: About 2500 BCE. In the valley of the Indus River, in what is now Pakistan, people built a city of brick with covered drains under its streets. Their writing has never been read.

paragraphs: Along a street of baked brick runs a drain. It is covered with more bricks, so the dirty water flows out of sight. Smaller drains come into it from the houses on each side. Many of the houses had a room with a brick floor for washing, and some had a toilet.
This was about 4,500 years ago.

The city is called Mohenjo-daro. Say "mo-HEN-jo DAH-ro." It stands beside the Indus River in what is now Pakistan. Tens of thousands of people may have lived there. Its streets were laid out in straight lines, and its bricks were made to the same proportions, as if everyone followed the same rules.
It was one of many cities along the Indus. They traded with cities as far away as Iraq.
So why don't we know more about them?
Because nobody can read what they wrote.

The people of the Indus carved signs on small square stones called seals, often above a picture of an animal. Thousands of seals have been found. There are about four hundred different signs. But most inscriptions are only four or five signs long, nobody knows what language they wrote, and no stone has been found with the same words in the Indus script and in a script we can read. Many people have claimed to read it. None has convinced the others.
So we can walk the streets of Mohenjo-daro and see how carefully it was built. We cannot read a single word its people left.
By about 1900 BCE, the city had been left empty, and nobody knows exactly why.
The seals are small enough to hold in your hand.

events.picturesWanted: a covered street drain at Mohenjo-daro; an Indus seal with a bull or "unicorn" and signs (National Museum of Pakistan, or Commons).

events.label: Campo del Cielo meteorites

place.name: Campo del Cielo, Chaco and Santiago del Estero provinces, Argentina (27.47 S, 60.58 W)

events.summary: About 2500 BCE. A mass of iron from space broke apart over what is now Argentina. Its pieces made a line of craters and left tonnes of iron in the ground.

paragraphs: In a field in northern Argentina lies a lump of metal as heavy as five elephants. It is dark and pitted, with smooth hollows like thumbprints. It is made of iron and nickel.
It came from space.

About 4,500 years ago, a mass of iron came down through the air over this plain. It broke apart as it fell. The pieces hit the ground along a line almost twenty kilometres long and made more than twenty craters. The biggest crater is more than a hundred metres across.
A piece of rock or metal from space that reaches the ground is called a meteorite. Iron meteorites are rare. Most meteorites that fall are stone.

The people who lived on the plain knew about the iron long before anyone wrote it down. In 1576, Spanish soldiers went looking for a great mass of iron that the local people used for their weapons. They found it. The Moqoit people, who still live there, call the place Piguen N'onaxa. The Spanish name, Campo del Cielo, means field of the sky.
How do we know when it fell?
Trees were burned when the pieces hit, and the charcoal has been dated. The dates cluster around 4,000 to 4,700 years ago. That is as close as anyone can get.

More than a hundred tonnes of the iron have been found, in pieces from the size of a pea to the size of a car. The largest, called Gancedo, weighs about thirty tonnes. It is the third-heaviest meteorite ever found.
The great irons still lie on the plain, and people can touch them.

events.picturesWanted: the El Chaco or Gancedo meteorite with people beside it for scale (Commons; licence to check).
references: William Cassidy, L. M. Villar, T. E. Bunch, T. P. Kohman and D. J. Milton, "Meteorites and craters of Campo del Cielo, Argentina," *Science*, 1965. The craters and the line they make.

events.label: Thera erupts

place.name: Thera (Santorini), in the Aegean Sea, Greece (36.40 N, 25.40 E)

events.summary: About 1600 BCE. The volcanic island of Thera, in the Aegean Sea, blew apart in one of the largest eruptions of the last ten thousand years. Its ash and waves reached Crete.

paragraphs: Today, big ships sail into a bay on the Greek island of Santorini and anchor in water hundreds of metres deep. Cliffs rise all around them, striped red, black and white.
The bay is the inside of a volcano.

About 3,600 years ago, the island, then called Thera, erupted. It threw out enough ash and rock to bury a large city many times over. When the eruption was over, the middle of the island had fallen in, and the sea poured into the hole.

People lived on Thera. Their town, now called Akrotiri, was buried in ash, and the ash kept it: houses two and three storeys high, with pictures painted on the walls of swallows, boys fishing and blue monkeys. Archaeologists have found almost no bodies there, and few valuable things. The people seem to have left in time. Where they went, nobody knows.
What happened to Crete?

Crete is a large island about 110 kilometres to the south. A people now called the Minoans lived there, in towns with great palaces. Ash from Thera fell on Crete. At Palaikastro, on Crete's eastern end, scientists have found a layer of sea sand, broken pottery and shells thrown far inland by a tsunami.

In 1939, a Greek archaeologist named Spyridon Marinatos suggested that the eruption destroyed the Minoans. It is a good story, and for a long time many people believed it. But digging since then shows that the Minoan palaces carried on for several generations after the eruption. They were hurt, but not destroyed. What finally ended them is still argued about.
Even the date is argued about. Some methods give about 1600 BCE. Others give about 1500. Scientists have been arguing for fifty years.
The ships anchor where the middle of the island used to be.

events.picturesWanted: the caldera from the cliffs; the swallows or "spring" fresco from Akrotiri (National Archaeological Museum, Athens; Commons).
references: Sturt Manning, "Eruption of Thera/Santorini," in Eric Cline, ed., *The Oxford Handbook of the Bronze Age Aegean* (2010). The eruption and its date.

events.label: Rhind papyrus

place.name: Thebes (Luxor), Egypt (25.70 N, 32.64 E)

events.summary: About 1550 BCE. In Egypt, a scribe named Ahmes copied out a scroll of arithmetic problems and their answers. It shows how Egyptians multiplied using nothing but doubling and adding.

paragraphs: A scroll of papyrus, a kind of paper made from reeds, is about five metres long. It begins with a promise: it will give "accurate reckoning for inquiring into things, and the knowledge of all things."
Then come more than eighty problems, with their answers.

The scribe who copied it wrote his name at the start: Ahmes. He says he copied it from an older scroll, written more than two hundred years before. That makes it one of the oldest books of mathematics in the world, and Ahmes one of the first people we know by name to have written mathematics down.
The problems are practical. How to share loaves of bread among ten men. How much grain fits in a round store. How steep to make the side of a pyramid.
How did an Egyptian scribe multiply?
By doubling. Suppose you want 13 times 12. Write 1 and 12. Double both: 2 and 24. Double again: 4 and 48. Again: 8 and 96. Stop there, because the next double, 16, is more than 13.
Now look down the left side for numbers that add up to 13. 1 and 4 and 8 make 13. Add the numbers beside them: 12 and 48 and 96. That makes 156, which is 13 times 12.

That is all there is to it. Nothing but doubling and adding, and no table of times to learn. It works for any two whole numbers, because every whole number can be made by adding some of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on.
In 1858 a Scottish lawyer named Alexander Henry Rhind bought the scroll in Luxor. That is why it carries his name instead of the scribe's.
It is in the British Museum. At the very start of the scroll, the scribe's name is still there: Ahmes.

events.label: Oldest written song

place.name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), on the coast of Syria (35.60 N, 35.78 E)

events.summary: About 1400 BCE. In the city of Ugarit, in what is now Syria, someone wrote a song on a clay tablet, with instructions for playing it. It is the oldest nearly complete written music we have.

paragraphs: A broken clay tablet has two parts, separated by a line. Above the line are the words of a song. Below the line are names and numbers.
The names and numbers are the music.

The tablet was found in the 1950s in the ruins of Ugarit, a port on the coast of what is now Syria. Say "OO-ga-rit." About 3,400 years ago, merchants there spoke and wrote in many languages. This song is in Hurrian, a language that is only partly understood today. It is a song to Nikkal, a goddess of orchards.

The instructions below the line are for a lyre. A lyre is a small stringed instrument, held in the arms. Its strings run from a sound box up to a crossbar. The instructions name pairs of strings, and each name is followed by a number. The names of the pairs are known from other tablets. So the tablet tells a player which strings to play, and something about how many times.
So what does it sound like?
That is the trouble. Nobody agrees.

We don't know how the lyre was tuned. We don't know whether each pair of strings was played together or one after the other. We don't know whether the numbers mean how many times to play, or something else. We don't know how the words fit the notes, or how fast it went.

Since the 1970s, several people have worked it out, each carefully, each in a different way. Their versions sound nothing alike. Some play the notes one after another, as a tune. Others play them two at a time.
Every recording you can find is someone's best guess.

events.label: Nok clay heads

place.name: the Nok region, Kaduna State, central Nigeria (9.50 N, 8.00 E)

events.summary: From about 900 BCE. In what is now central Nigeria, people made life-size clay heads with carefully shaped eyes and hair. They are among the oldest large sculptures from Africa south of the Sahara.

paragraphs: A clay head, about as big as a real one, looks straight ahead. Its eyes are shaped like triangles, with a hole in the middle of each for the pupil. Its hair is piled up in neat rolls and buns. Someone spent a long time on it.
It is between two and three thousand years old.

In 1943, men digging for tin near the village of Nok, in central Nigeria, found a clay head in the gravel. A clerk at the mine took it home and used it as a scarecrow in a yam field for a year. Then a young archaeologist named Bernard Fagg saw it. Since then, hundreds of heads and parts of figures have been found across the region.
Nok is the name of the village. It is not the name of the people who made the heads.
What do we know about them?

They farmed pearl millet and cowpeas. They were among the first people in West Africa to make iron, heating rock in clay furnaces until the metal ran out. Their figures were hollow, built up from coils of clay and then carved, with walls thin enough to fire without cracking. Almost none has been found whole.

Most of what we don't know was lost more recently. For fifty years, Nok figures have been dug up and sold to collectors. When a figure is pulled out of the ground in a hurry, nobody writes down where it was, what lay beside it, or how deep it was buried. The figure survives. The answers to how it was used do not.
Were the heads portraits? Were they made for the dead? Nobody knows.
Nobody knows what the people who made them called themselves.

events.label: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga

place.name: Nukuleka, Tongatapu, Tonga (21.13 S, 175.15 W)

events.summary: About 850 BCE. Sailors from the islands near New Guinea, whose pottery is called Lapita, reached Tonga, in the middle of the Pacific. No human had ever set foot there before.

paragraphs: A piece of broken pottery lies on a beach in Tonga. Its surface is covered with fine patterns: rows of tiny dots, pressed into the wet clay with a toothed stamp before it was fired.
Pottery with these patterns has been found on islands across more than four thousand kilometres of the Pacific.

It is called Lapita pottery, after a beach in New Caledonia where it was dug up in 1952. The people who made it lived at first on the islands near New Guinea. Then, a little more than three thousand years ago, they began to sail east.

East of the Solomon Islands, the islands get farther apart. Before then, people had crossed plenty of sea, but usually with the next island in sight or nearly so. The Lapita sailors went where no land could be seen, and kept going. From Vanuatu to Fiji is about 850 kilometres of open water.
How do you find an island you have never seen?

Nobody knows exactly how the Lapita sailors did it. Later Pacific navigators found their way by the stars, the shape of the waves, the clouds that gather over land, and birds that fly out to fish and back to land at night. The Lapita sailors probably knew some of the same things.
They did not travel light. They brought pigs, dogs and chickens, and plants to grow: taro, yams, breadfruit. Everywhere they landed, they were the first people ever to live there.
About 2,850 years ago they reached Tonga. At a place called Nukuleka, archaeologists have found some of the oldest Lapita pottery in Tonga, dated by the coral tools buried with it.
Their descendants kept sailing. Over the next two thousand years, they reached Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island.

references: Patrick Kirch, *On the Road of the Winds: An Archaeological History of the Pacific Islands* (University of California Press, 2nd ed., 2017). The Lapita spread.
David Burley and others, "High precision U/Th dating of first Polynesian settlement," *PLoS ONE*, 2012. Nukuleka and its date.
Geoffrey Irwin, *The Prehistoric Exploration and Colonisation of the Pacific* (Cambridge, 1992). Navigation and why the sailors went east.

events.label: Homer written down

place.name: Greece; the exact place is unknown (38.0 N, 23.7 E marks Athens, where a written version is later reported)
place.note: marks Athens, where a written version is later reported

events.summary: 700s or 600s BCE. Homer is thought to have been a travelling poet who recited stories about the Trojan War. Around this time, his stories were first written down.

paragraphs: A long poem called the Iliad tells about a few weeks near the end of a war at a city called Troy. It is more than fifteen thousand lines long. Another, the Odyssey, tells about a soldier's ten-year journey home from that war. It is about twelve thousand lines.
For a long time, nobody wrote them down.

The Greeks said both poems were made by a poet called Homer. Nobody knows who Homer was, when he lived, or whether he was one person. What seems likely is that poems like these were sung by travelling poets, who performed them from memory to anyone who would listen.
How could anyone remember fifteen thousand lines?

In the 1930s, an American scholar named Milman Parry went to the mountains of what was then Yugoslavia. There he met singers who could not read or write, and who sang long poems about old wars, some as long as the Odyssey. They did not memorise the words exactly. They knew thousands of ready-made phrases and scenes, and they rebuilt the poem each time they sang it. The Iliad is full of the same kind of phrases: "rosy-fingered dawn," "swift-footed Achilles."
The Greeks had begun writing with an alphabet not long before, around 800 BCE. At some point in the next two hundred years, someone wrote the poems down. Nobody knows who, or exactly when.

That first written copy is lost. The oldest pieces we have were found in Egypt, on scraps of papyrus about four hundred years younger. The oldest complete copy of the Iliad was made about 1,200 years after that, in the 900s.
It is in a library in Venice.

events.picturesWanted: a page of the Venetus A manuscript (Biblioteca Marciana, Venice; Homer Multitext images are CC BY-NC-SA, non-commercial only).
references: Milman Parry, *The Making of Homeric Verse: The Collected Papers of Milman Parry*, ed. Adam Parry (Oxford, 1971). The singers and the phrases.
Albert Lord, *The Singer of Tales* (Harvard, 1960). Parry's work with the singers, written up by his assistant.
Barry Powell, *Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet* (Cambridge, 1991). The alphabet and when the poems could have been written.
The Homer Multitext project (homermultitext.org). The Venetus A manuscript.

events.label: Eclipse stops a battle

place.name: the Halys river (now the Kızılırmak), central Turkey. The battlefield itself is not known.

events.summary: 28 May 585 BCE. During a battle between two kings in what is now Turkey, the Moon covered the Sun and the day went dark. The armies stopped fighting, and the kings made peace.

paragraphs: Two armies were fighting beside a river in what is now Turkey when darkness fell. It was evening, but the Sun had not yet set. The day had turned into night.

The cause was an eclipse. In this case, the Moon moved in front of the Sun. That cast the Moon's shadow on parts of the Earth, including the battlefield. When the Moon covers the whole Sun, stars come out and birds go silent.
Probably no one in either army knew why the Sun seemed to go out, but the sudden and mysterious darkness stopped the fighting.

The armies belonged to two kings. Alyattes ruled the Lydians, to the west of the river. Cyaxares ruled the Medes, to the east. They had been at war for five years. This was the sixth. No one knows how many soldiers died in those wars or what the fighting cost.

The eclipse ended the fighting that day, and soon afterwards the two kings made peace. The river, called the Halys, became the border between their kingdoms, and a daughter of Alyattes married a son of Cyaxares.

We know about the battle from Herodotus, a Greek historian who wrote a long history about 150 years later. Herodotus also says that a man named Thales had told the Greeks the eclipse would come that year. Most people who study this doubt it. In Thales's time nobody knew how to work out when an eclipse would happen.

We know the day all this happened, though Herodotus did not tell us. The date comes from the sky. The Moon and the Earth move so regularly that astronomers can work backwards and find every eclipse that ever crossed that part of the world. Only one fits: 28 May 585 BCE, in the evening.
The battle is often called the earliest event in history whose exact day we know.

events.picturesWanted: a photograph of a total eclipse of the Sun; a map of the eclipse's path across Anatolia, if a good one with a clear licence exists.
references: Herodotus, *Histories*, Book 1, section 74 (about 430 BCE). The only ancient account. Free online at the Perseus Digital Library.
F. Richard Stephenson, *Historical Eclipses and Earth's Rotation* (Cambridge University Press, 1997). Dating ancient eclipses, and why the Earth's slowing spin matters.

events.label: Ashoka and the Kalinga war

place.name: Kalinga (now Odisha), eastern India; Dhauli, near Bhubaneswar, marks it (20.19 N, 85.84 E)

events.summary: 261 BCE. King Ashoka of India conquered the land of Kalinga. Afterwards he had the cost of the war carved on rock, said he regretted it, and changed how he ruled.

paragraphs: A message from a king is carved on a rock face in India. Part of it reads:
"One hundred and fifty thousand people were deported, one hundred thousand were killed, and many times that number perished."
The king is talking about his own war.
His name was Ashoka. Say "a-SHOH-ka." He ruled most of India. About 2,300 years ago, eight years after he became king, he invaded Kalinga, a land on the east coast of India, and won.

Kings of that time carved their victories on stone. Ashoka carved something else. He said the killing and the suffering of the families filled him with sorrow and regret. He said that from then on, the only conquest worth making was a conquest by what he called dhamma: doing right by others. He turned seriously to Buddhism, stopped making war, and had messages carved on rocks and tall stone pillars across his kingdom.
What did his messages say?

Treat servants and workers fairly. Respect your parents. Respect the beliefs of others. Don't kill animals needlessly. Plant trees along roads for shade, and dig wells. He wrote that he had set up care for sick people and sick animals.

What did the war cost? Only Ashoka's own numbers survive. Nobody else counted, and there is no way to check them. We don't know what the war cost in money or effort. We know it made him change how he ruled.
After Ashoka, his writing was forgotten. For two thousand years nobody could read it. In 1837, a scholar named James Prinsep worked out the letters.
The rocks inside Kalinga itself carry Ashoka's messages too. On them, the passage counting the dead is left out.

events.picturesWanted: the Dhauli rock inscription; the lion capital from one of Ashoka's pillars (Sarnath Museum; Commons).
references: Ashoka, Major Rock Edict XIII. Translation in Romila Thapar, *Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas* (Oxford, 1961; revised 1997). The numbers and the regret.
Nayanjot Lahiri, *Ashoka in Ancient India* (Harvard, 2015). His life and the edicts.
Charles Allen, *Ashoka: The Search for India's Lost Emperor* (Little, Brown, 2012). Prinsep and the decipherment.

events.label: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
events.kindNote: not in the closed list (sky, earth, crop, craft, object, place, person, text); kept as written

place.name: Alexandria, Egypt (31.20 N, 29.92 E), with Syene (Aswan) to the south

events.summary: About 240 BCE. In Alexandria, in Egypt, a scholar named Eratosthenes worked out the size of the whole Earth from the length of a shadow and the distance between two cities.

paragraphs: In the town of Syene, in the south of Egypt, there was said to be a deep well. On one day a year, at noon, the Sun shone straight down into it and lit the water at the bottom. On that day the Sun was directly overhead, and a stick standing upright cast no shadow at all.
On the same day, at noon, in Alexandria, far to the north, an upright stick did cast a shadow.
Why the difference?

Eratosthenes thought he knew. He was the chief librarian at Alexandria, in charge of the greatest library of the time. Like other Greek scholars, he took it that the Earth is a ball, and that the Sun is so far away that its rays arrive side by side. If the ground were flat, the stick in Alexandria would cast no shadow either. The shadow meant the ground between the two cities curved.

So he measured how much. The shadow in Alexandria showed that the Sun was one fiftieth of a full circle away from straight overhead. So the distance from Alexandria to Syene had to be one fiftieth of the way around the Earth.
That distance was known: about 5,000 stadia. A stadion was a Greek unit of length, about the length of a running track. Fifty times 5,000 is 250,000 stadia. That was his size for the whole Earth.
How close did he come?

Nobody knows exactly. There were several different stadia in use, of different lengths, and nobody knows which one he meant. Depending on the answer, he was within about two percent of the true size, or about sixteen percent too big. Either way, one man with a stick and a known distance had measured the whole Earth without leaving Egypt.
His own book is lost. We know his method from a writer named Cleomedes, who described it about three hundred years later.

events.picturesWanted: a simple drawing of the two sticks and the Sun's parallel rays (to be drawn for CW; a live version belongs on the plane).
references: Cleomedes, *On the Heavens*, Book 1, chapter 7. Translation in Alan Bowen and Robert Todd, *Cleomedes' Lectures on Astronomy* (University of California Press, 2004). The only full account of the method.
Juergen Dutka, "Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth reconsidered," *Archive for History of Exact Sciences*, 1993. Stadia and accuracy.
Duane Roller, *Eratosthenes' Geography* (Princeton, 2010). His life and lost work.

events.label: Antikythera mechanism

place.name: the Antikythera wreck, off the island of Antikythera, Greece (35.89 N, 23.30 E)

events.summary: About 100 BCE. A Greek ship sank carrying a box of bronze gears that showed the movements of the Sun and Moon and predicted eclipses. Nothing like it is known again for over a thousand years.

paragraphs: A lump of green, crumbling bronze sits in a museum in Athens. On one side, if you look closely, you can see the teeth of a gear wheel about as wide as your hand.
Nobody expected gears from ancient Greece.

In 1900, sponge divers sheltering from a storm off the small island of Antikythera found a shipwreck on the sea floor. Over the next year they brought up bronze and marble statues, glass, pottery and coins. The ship had sunk about 2,100 years ago. The lump of bronze came up with everything else, and for months nobody paid it much attention. Then, in 1902, it split open, and an archaeologist named Valerios Stais saw the gear.
What was it?

It took most of the next century to find out. From the 1950s, a scientist named Derek de Solla Price studied it, and in the 1970s he had it X-rayed. In 2005, a team scanned the pieces in layers, the way a hospital scans a body, and read writing on them that had been hidden for two thousand years.

It had been a wooden box about the size of a shoebox, with a handle on the side. Turning the handle turned dozens of bronze gears inside. About thirty survive. On the front, pointers showed where the Sun and Moon were among the stars, and a little ball, half silver and half dark, turned to show the phase of the Moon. On the back, dials showed which months would have an eclipse, and when the great athletic games were held.
Nobody knows who made it. Nobody knows who it was for, or where the ship was going with it.
No machine with gears this fine is known again for more than a thousand years.

events.picturesWanted: the main fragment showing the large gear (National Archaeological Museum, Athens; Commons); a reconstruction drawing (licence to check).
references: Derek de Solla Price, *Gears from the Greeks: The Antikythera Mechanism, a Calendar Computer from ca. 80 B.C.* (American Philosophical Society, 1974). The X-ray work.
Tony Freeth and others, "Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism," *Nature*, 2006. The 2005 scans and the inscriptions.
Tony Freeth and others, "A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism," *Scientific Reports*, 2021. The front display.
Alexander Jones, *A Portable Cosmos* (Oxford, 2017). The whole story, readable.

events.label: Vesuvius buries Pompeii

place.name: Pompeii, near Naples, Italy (40.75 N, 14.49 E)

events.summary: 79 CE. The volcano Vesuvius, near Naples in Italy, erupted and buried the town of Pompeii under ash and stone. A seventeen-year-old named Pliny watched from across the bay and later described it.

paragraphs: A young man is staying in a house across the bay from a mountain. One afternoon his mother points out a strange cloud rising over the mountain. He says it looks like an umbrella pine: a tall trunk, spreading out at the top into branches.
He was seventeen. His name was Pliny.
The mountain was Vesuvius, near Naples in Italy. Few people then thought of it as a volcano. Its slopes were covered with vineyards, and the town of Pompeii sat a few kilometres from its foot.

We know what Pliny saw because, about twenty-five years later, a historian named Tacitus asked him for it, and Pliny wrote two letters. The letters survive. They are the only eyewitness account of the eruption that survives.

His uncle, also named Pliny, commanded the Roman fleet in the bay. He sailed across toward the mountain to rescue people on the shore. He never came back. His nephew stayed behind, and the next day, with his mother, joined the crowds leaving town as ash fell and the ground shook. He writes that the darkness was "not the dark of a moonless or cloudy night, but as if the lamp had been put out in a closed room."

Pompeii was buried under several metres of ash and small stones. Nearby, the town of Herculaneum was buried deeper, under hot flows of ash and gas that ran down the mountain. Many people escaped. Many did not.
Then the towns were forgotten. Digging at Pompeii began in 1748, more than 1,600 years later. The streets, shops, paintings, bread in the ovens and words scratched on walls were all still there.
The date is argued about. Copies of Pliny's letters say 24 August, but a note scratched in charcoal, found in Pompeii in 2018, suggests the autumn.
Volcanologists still call a tall eruption like this one "Plinian," after the young man who described it.

events.picturesWanted: a Pompeii street with Vesuvius behind it (Commons); a wall painting from Pompeii.
references: Pliny the Younger, *Letters*, Book 6, letters 16 and 20, to Tacitus. Translation by Betty Radice (Penguin, 1963). The eyewitness account and the quoted line.
Mary Beard, *Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town* (Profile, 2008). The town and its rediscovery.
Haraldur Sigurdsson and others, "The eruption of Vesuvius in A.D. 79," *National Geographic Research*, 1985. The eruption's stages.
Massimo Osanna, reports on the 2018 charcoal inscription (Parco Archeologico di Pompei). The date argument.

events.label: Zhang Heng's earthquake jar

place.name: Luoyang, China (34.62 N, 112.45 E)

events.summary: 132 CE. At the Han court in Luoyang, China, an astronomer named Zhang Heng built a bronze jar that dropped a ball when the ground shook, even from an earthquake too far away to feel.

paragraphs: A bronze jar nearly two metres across stands in a room at the emperor's court. Around its outside are eight dragons, facing eight directions. Each dragon holds a bronze ball in its mouth. Below each dragon sits a bronze toad, looking up, with its mouth open.
One day a ball drops into a toad's mouth with a clang.
Nobody in the room has felt anything.

The jar was made in 132 by Zhang Heng, an astronomer and mathematician at the court of the Han dynasty in Luoyang, China. Say "JAHNG HUNG." China has many earthquakes, and the court wanted to know about them quickly.

According to the history of the time, the jar was built so that when the ground shook, something inside tipped, and one dragon let go of its ball. The toad that caught the ball showed which direction the shaking came from.
Did it work?

The same history tells this story. One day a ball dropped, and no one had felt any earthquake. The scholars at court said the jar had failed. A few days later a messenger arrived. There had been an earthquake in Longxi, far to the west. After that, everyone believed in it.
What was inside the jar?

Nobody knows. The jar is lost. All that survives is a short description, written down about three hundred years later, and it does not say how the inside worked. Scientists in China and elsewhere have built models since the 1950s, most with a heavy weight hanging inside like a pendulum. Some of the models work. Nobody knows whether any of them is how Zhang Heng did it.
Zhang Heng also made a globe of the stars, turned by water, and counted 2,500 stars in the sky, not including thousands of very faint ones.
All that is left of the jar is one paragraph.

events.picturesWanted: a modern replica of the jar (several museums; Commons; the caption must say it is a modern model).
references: *Hou Hanshu* (Book of the Later Han), biography of Zhang Heng, compiled by Fan Ye in the 400s. The only description and the Longxi story.
Joseph Needham and Wang Ling, *Science and Civilisation in China*, vol. 3 (Cambridge, 1959). Translation and discussion.
Hong-sen Yan and Kuo-Hung Hsiao, "Reconstruction design of the lost seismoscope of ancient China," *Mechanism and Machine Theory*, 2007. The modern models.

events.label: Diamond Sutra, the oldest dated printed book

place.name: found in the Mogao Caves, Dunhuang, China (40.04 N, 94.81 E)

events.summary: 11 May 868. In China, a man named Wang Jie paid to have a book printed from carved wooden blocks. It is the oldest printed book that carries its own date.

paragraphs: At the end of a paper scroll, about five metres long, there is a line of writing:
"Reverently made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two parents, on the fifteenth day of the fourth moon of the ninth year of Xiantong."
That day was 11 May 868.
The scroll is a copy of a Buddhist teaching called the Diamond Sutra. It was not written by hand. It was printed.
How do you print a book without a printing press?

You write out the page in ink on thin paper. You lay the paper face down on a smooth block of wood, so the writing shows through backwards. Then you carve away all the wood around the letters, leaving them standing up. Ink the block, press a sheet of paper on it, and you have a page. You can print it as many times as you like. The Diamond Sutra was printed from seven blocks, one for each sheet, and the sheets were glued end to end. The first sheet is a picture.

The printing is so clean that it was not a first try. People in China had been printing from blocks for a long time before 868. But this is the oldest printed book we have that tells us exactly when it was made.

It was found in a cave. Near the town of Dunhuang, in western China, hundreds of caves were cut into a cliff and painted inside. Around the year 1000, someone filled a small side cave with tens of thousands of scrolls and paintings and walled it up. Nobody knows why.
In 1900, a man looking after the caves found the hidden door. The scroll is now in the British Library in London.
It was printed nearly six hundred years before Gutenberg, in Germany, printed his Bible.
Wang Jie made it to be given away, for his mother and father.

events.picturesWanted: the frontispiece and the colophon (British Library, Or.8210/P.2; released for reuse).
references: British Library, "The Diamond Sutra," Or.8210/P.2 (bl.uk and the International Dunhuang Project, idp.bl.uk). The colophon, its translation and date.
Frances Wood and Mark Barnard, *The Diamond Sutra: The Story of the World's Earliest Dated Printed Book* (British Library, 2010). How it was made and found.
Valerie Hansen, *The Silk Road: A New History* (Oxford, 2012), chapter on Dunhuang. The sealed cave.

events.label: The guest star of 1054

place.name: recorded at Kaifeng, China (34.80 N, 114.35 E); the star itself is in the constellation Taurus

events.summary: 4 July 1054. Astronomers in China recorded a new star, bright enough to see in daylight for more than three weeks. What is left of it is the Crab Nebula.

paragraphs: A report from the court astronomers of China, in the summer of 1054:

A guest star had appeared at dawn in the east, a little to the south-east of a star we now call Zeta Tauri. It was bright enough to see in daylight, like Venus, with rays of light pointing out on all sides.
A guest star was the Chinese name for a star that appears where there was none before, stays a while, and goes.
The astronomers kept watching. For twenty-three days it could be seen in daylight. It stayed visible at night for almost two years. Then it faded out.
What had they seen?

A star exploding. When a very large star runs out of fuel, its middle collapses and the rest of it blows apart. For a few weeks the explosion can outshine a whole galaxy. This is called a supernova. The star had not appeared. It had been there all along, too faint to see, until it blew up.
Nobody in 1054 could have known that.

In the 1700s and 1800s, astronomers with telescopes found a faint, cloudy patch in the same part of the sky. In the 1840s, an Irish astronomer drew it, and it looked to him like a crab. It has been called the Crab Nebula ever since. A nebula is a cloud in space. In the 1920s, astronomers noticed that the cloud was growing. Measuring how fast, and working backwards, they found it must have started growing about nine hundred years before.
The Crab Nebula is what is left of the guest star.
It is so far away that its light takes about six thousand five hundred years to reach us. So the star really blew up about six thousand five hundred years before the astronomers saw it.
The cloud is still growing, by more than a thousand kilometres every second.

events.picturesWanted: the Crab Nebula (Hubble or Webb images, NASA/ESA, public domain); Lord Rosse's 1844 drawing.
references: *Song Huiyao* and *Songshi* (History of the Song), astronomy chapters. The report. Translated in Richard Stephenson and David Green, *Historical Supernovae and Their Remnants* (Oxford, 2002).

NASA, "Crab Nebula" (science.nasa.gov). Distance and expansion.

events.label: Great Zimbabwe

place.name: Great Zimbabwe, near Masvingo, Zimbabwe (20.27 S, 30.93 E)

events.summary: About 1300. In southern Africa, the builders of Great Zimbabwe raised walls of fitted granite as high as eleven metres, without mortar. Later, outsiders claimed Africans could not have built them.

paragraphs: A curving wall of granite blocks stands on a plain in southern Africa. It is more than two hundred and fifty metres long, and in places eleven metres high and five metres thick. No mortar holds the blocks together. They are cut and fitted so well that they have stood for about seven hundred years.
Inside the wall stands a solid tower of stone, shaped like a cone.

This is Great Zimbabwe. It was the centre of a kingdom that grew rich trading gold. Its gold went to towns on the coast of East Africa, and from there across the Indian Ocean. At Great Zimbabwe, archaeologists have found glass beads from India, pottery from China and Persia, and a coin from the coastal city of Kilwa. Perhaps ten thousand people lived there at its height.
Who built it?
The ancestors of the Shona people, who live in Zimbabwe today. Archaeologists agree on this, and have for about a hundred years.
But for a long time, many Europeans refused to believe it.

From the 1870s on, some of the Europeans who came said the walls must have been built by outsiders: by people from the Bible, or by traders from the Mediterranean. They had no evidence for this. They simply did not believe Africans could have built something so grand. Some dug up the site looking for proof and threw away what they found, destroying evidence as they went.

In 1905, and again in 1929, archaeologists who dug carefully showed that everything they found was African. Even so, the government of the country, run by white settlers, kept the old story alive in guidebooks and school books all through the 1960s and 1970s.
In 1980, the country became independent. It took its new name from the ruins: Zimbabwe, from a Shona word for houses of stone.

references: Peter Garlake, *Great Zimbabwe* (Thames & Hudson, 1973). The site and the history of the argument.
Gertrude Caton-Thompson, *The Zimbabwe Culture: Ruins and Reactions* (Oxford, 1931). The 1929 excavation.
Innocent Pikirayi, *The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States* (AltaMira, 2001). The kingdom and its trade.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Great Zimbabwe National Monument." Dimensions and dates.

events.label: Chillies reach Asia

place.name: Goa, on the west coast of India (15.50 N, 73.83 E)

events.summary: 1500s. Portuguese ships carried chilli peppers from the Americas to Goa, in India. Within a century chillies were growing across Asia, in places whose cooking now seems impossible without them.

paragraphs: A bowl of curry in southern India. A plate of noodles in Thailand. A pot of kimchi in Korea. All three are hot with chilli.
Five hundred years ago, none of them was.
Chilli peppers come from the Americas. People in the Americas were growing them at least six thousand years ago. Nobody in Asia, Africa or Europe had ever tasted one.

Then, in 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west, looking for a way to India and its spices. One of the spices he wanted was black pepper. He never reached India, but in the Caribbean he found a plant whose fruit burned the mouth, and he called it pepper too. That is why chillies are still called peppers, though they are not related to black pepper at all.

Portuguese sailors carried chillies around Africa to their trading town of Goa, on the west coast of India. Chillies are easy to grow. You need only a few seeds, and a plant fruits in months. Farmers planted them, traders carried the seeds on, and within about a hundred years chillies were growing across India, and in Southeast Asia and China too.

Nobody wrote down the day the first chilli arrived. One of the earliest mentions in India is in a song by a poet named Purandara Dasa, who lived in the 1500s. He calls the chilli the saviour of the poor, because it made plain food taste good.
In Korea, red chilli in kimchi came later still, in the 1700s, and became common only in the 1800s.
So the cooking that tastes oldest in many parts of Asia uses a plant that arrived only a few lifetimes ago.
Today India grows more chillies than any other country.

events.picturesWanted: chilli plants with ripe fruit; a spice market in India (Commons).
references: Linda Perry and others, "Starch fossils and the domestication and dispersal of chili peppers (Capsicum spp. L.) in the Americas," *Science*, 2007. The age of chillies in the Americas.
Lizzie Collingham, *Curry: A Tale of Cooks and Conquerors* (Oxford, 2006). Chillies reaching India.
Jean Andrews, *Peppers: The Domesticated Capsicums* (University of Texas Press, 1995). How chillies spread.
FAOSTAT (Food and Agriculture Organization). India as the largest producer.

events.label: Silver mountain at Potosí

place.name: Potosí, Bolivia (19.59 S, 65.75 W)

events.summary: 1545. High in the Andes, in what is now Bolivia, Spanish colonists began mining a mountain made rich with silver. Its silver changed prices as far away as China. The miners paid a terrible price.

paragraphs: A red-brown mountain rises above a city in the Andes. It is called Cerro Rico, the Rich Hill. Inside, it is full of tunnels, so many that its top has begun to sink.
It is still being mined, almost five hundred years later.

In 1545, Spanish colonists in the Andes learned of silver in this mountain. The ore near the top was so rich that silver could be melted straight out of it. Within thirty years, the town at its foot, Potosí, had become one of the biggest cities in the Americas. It stands about 4,000 metres high, where the air is thin and nothing much grows.
Where did the silver go?

Some went across the Atlantic to Spain. A great deal ended up in China. At that time the Chinese government collected its taxes in silver, and China needed more silver than it had. From 1571, Spanish ships carried American silver across the Pacific to Manila, in the Philippines, where Chinese merchants traded silk and porcelain for it. For the first time, goods went all the way around the world.
Who dug it out?

From 1573, the Spanish rulers forced Indigenous men from across the Andes to take turns working in the mines. The system was called the mita. Miners worked deep underground for days at a time, carrying heavy loads up ladders. Silver was separated from the rock with mercury, which is poisonous. Many men died. Many families left their villages to escape the mita.
How many died? Nobody counted. Some writers give huge numbers, but nobody can check them, and historians disagree.
In Spanish there is still a saying for something priceless: "vale un Potosí," it's worth a Potosí.

events.picturesWanted: Cerro Rico above the city (Commons); an early drawing of the mountain from 1553 by Pedro Cieza de León (public domain).
references: Kris Lane, *Potosí: The Silver City That Changed the World* (University of California Press, 2019). The whole story.
Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez, "Born with a 'silver spoon': the origin of world trade in 1571," *Journal of World History*, 1995. Silver to China through Manila.
Jeffrey Cole, *The Potosí Mita, 1573–1700* (Stanford, 1985). The forced labour.

events.label: Timbuktu's books

place.name: Timbuktu, Mali (16.77 N, 3.01 W)

events.summary: 1500s. Timbuktu, a trading town at the edge of the Sahara, in what is now Mali, was full of scholars and books. Families there kept hundreds of thousands of handwritten books for centuries.

paragraphs: In 2012, men with guns took over the town of Timbuktu, at the southern edge of the Sahara desert. Soon afterwards, a librarian named Abdel Kader Haidara began packing books into metal trunks.

He and his helpers moved them at night, a few trunks at a time, by donkey cart, car and boat, hundreds of kilometres south to the city of Bamako. By the time they were done, they had moved more than three hundred thousand books.
Why were there so many books in a desert town?

Five hundred years ago, Timbuktu was rich. It stood where camel caravans crossing the Sahara met boats on the Niger River. Salt came from the north, and gold from the south, and with them came scholars. In the 1500s, Timbuktu had schools full of students, and families who collected books and passed them down.

The books were written by hand, mostly in Arabic, some in local languages written in Arabic letters. They are about astronomy, arithmetic, medicine, law, grammar, poetry, the history of the region, and how to settle a quarrel. One scholar of the town, Ahmed Baba, wrote more than forty books and said his own library of about 1,600 was one of the smaller ones in his family.
Paper, ink and bindings were precious. Families kept the books in wooden chests and mud-brick rooms, and many survived for four or five hundred years.
In January 2013, as the armed men left, they set fire to a library. About four thousand books were burned or lost. Most of the rest were already gone, in trunks, in Bamako.
Nobody knows exactly how many books there are. Many families still keep theirs private.

events.label: Florentine Codex

place.name: Tlatelolco, now part of Mexico City (19.45 N, 99.14 W). The finished copy is in Florence.

events.summary: 1577. In Mexico, Nahua scholars and a Spanish friar finished twelve books describing the Aztec world, in the Aztecs' own language and pictures. The Spanish conquest had ended that world fifty years earlier.

paragraphs: A page shows a small painted picture of people at work. Beside the picture are two columns of writing. The left column is in Spanish. The right column is in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. Say "NAH-wah-tl."
There are about 2,500 pages like it, and nearly as many pictures.

The book was made in Mexico between the 1540s and 1577. Fifty years before, the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, had been a city of perhaps two hundred thousand people, built on a lake. In 1521, Spanish soldiers and their Indigenous allies destroyed it. Disease killed far more people than the fighting did.

A Spanish friar named Bernardino de Sahagún wanted to know what the Aztec world had been like. Partly this was so that missionaries would understand the people they were trying to convert. Partly he was simply fascinated. He asked Nahua elders who remembered the old days, and young Nahua scholars who could write both languages, to help him.
What did they write about?

Everything. The gods and festivals. The stars. The plants and animals of Mexico, hundreds of them, with pictures. How to raise a child. What merchants did. How feather workers made their cloaks. Speeches parents gave their children. The last of the twelve books tells the story of the conquest, from the side of the people who lost.
The Nahua artists drew the pictures. Some of them had been trained in the old way of painting books before the Spanish came.
The finished copy went to Spain, and from there, somehow, to Florence, in Italy. That is why it is called the Florentine Codex. A codex is a handwritten book.
In 2023 the whole book was put online, free for anyone to read.

events.label: Huaynaputina erupts

place.name: Huaynaputina, southern Peru (16.61 S, 70.85 W)

events.summary: 19 February 1600. A volcano in southern Peru erupted in the largest eruption in South America's recorded history. Its ash cooled the whole world, and the next year's summer in Europe and Russia was bitterly cold.

paragraphs: In the Andes of southern Peru there is a mountain that hardly looks like a volcano. It has no tall cone. Before 1600, the people living nearby did not know it was one.
On 19 February 1600, it exploded.

Ash and rock fell over the countryside for days. Villages around the mountain were buried. In the city of Arequipa, about seventy kilometres away, ash lay thick on the roofs, and it was dark in the middle of the day. The rivers ran with mud. Around 1,500 people died.
Then something happened much farther away.
A large eruption throws a fine mist high into the sky, higher than any clouds. The mist spreads around the whole world and blocks a little sunlight. For a year or two, the world is cooler.

In 1601, the summer in much of Europe and Asia was one of the coldest in six hundred years. We know this because trees grow less in a cold year, and their growth rings for 1601 are thin. In France the grapes ripened late. In Russia, the harvest failed that year, and the next, and the one after. About two million people died in the famine that followed.
Did the volcano cause the Russian famine? Many scientists think it helped. The cold year matches. But crops fail for many reasons, and nobody can be sure.
This is the same thing that happened after the eruption of Tambora, in Indonesia, 215 years later, when Europe had a year without a summer.
The mountain's name is from Quechua, the language of the Andes. Say "WHY-na-poo-TEE-na." It is often translated as "young volcano" or "new volcano."

events.label: Taj Mahal

place.name: Agra, India (27.18 N, 78.04 E)

events.summary: About 1653. In Agra, India, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan finished a white marble tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It took about twenty years and many thousands of workers.

paragraphs: A white building stands at the end of a long garden, beside a river. It has a great dome, four smaller domes, and a tall thin tower at each corner. From the front, its left half is a mirror of its right half. So is the garden. So are the buildings on either side.
It is a tomb.

In 1631, Mumtaz Mahal, the wife of the emperor Shah Jahan, died giving birth to their fourteenth child. Shah Jahan ruled the Mughal Empire, which covered most of northern India. The next year he began building her tomb in the city of Agra.

It took about twenty years. The white marble came from quarries about 400 kilometres away. It is said that more than a thousand elephants carried materials, and that about twenty thousand people worked on it: masons, carvers, painters, and craftsmen from as far away as Persia and Central Asia. Nobody knows the true numbers.

Look closely at the walls and you find flowers made of stone. Workers cut thin pieces of coloured stone, such as jade, carnelian and lapis lazuli, and fitted them into shapes cut in the marble, so tightly that you can barely feel the joins.
The four towers at the corners lean very slightly outward. One common explanation is that if an earthquake knocked one down, it would fall away from the tomb.
Shah Jahan did not have a happy old age. In 1658 his son took the throne and kept him locked up in the fort at Agra. From there he could see the Taj Mahal, further along the river. He died in 1666.
He was buried beside her. In the whole building, his tomb is the only thing that is not placed in perfect symmetry.

events.label: The last dodo

place.name: Mauritius, in the Indian Ocean (20.20 S, 57.50 E)

events.summary: 1662. Sailors shipwrecked on the island of Mauritius, in the Indian Ocean, reported seeing dodos. It is the last sighting most scientists accept. Less than a hundred years after the first Dutch ships, the bird was gone.

paragraphs: A large grey bird stands on a beach. It is about a metre tall, with a huge hooked beak, tiny wings and a tuft of curly feathers for a tail. It cannot fly. It has never needed to.
It is a dodo, and it lives only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean.

For millions of years, no people, cats, rats or pigs lived on Mauritius. A bird that nested on the ground and could not fly was safe. The dodo's closest living relatives are pigeons. Its ancestors probably flew to the island, and over a very long time, with nothing to fly away from, their descendants lost the use of their wings.

Dutch sailors began stopping at Mauritius in 1598. They ate dodos, though they complained about the taste. They also brought animals: rats that came ashore from the ships, and pigs and monkeys that they let loose. These ate the dodos' eggs and chicks.

In 1662, a Dutch sailor named Volkert Evertsz, shipwrecked on the island, reported catching dodos on a small islet off the coast. It is the last sighting most scientists accept. By about 1690, there were none.
What did a dodo really look like?

Nobody knows exactly. The famous paintings show a round, fat bird. But some of those painters worked from dodos that had been overfed on ships, or from stuffed birds, or from other paintings. From its bones, scientists now think the living bird was slimmer.
Almost nothing of the bird itself survives: skeletons, pieced together from bones dug out of a swamp on Mauritius in the 1860s, and one dried head and one foot, in a museum in Oxford.
That head and foot hold the only dodo skin left in the world.

events.label: Sangaku, geometry for the shrines

place.name: Japan; the oldest surviving tablet is in Tochigi Prefecture (36.57 N, 139.88 E)

events.summary: From the 1680s. In Japan, people began hanging painted wooden tablets of geometry puzzles in shrines and temples. Farmers, samurai, women and children made them. About nine hundred survive.

paragraphs: Under the roof of a shrine in Japan hangs a wooden board, painted in bright colours. On it are circles inside a triangle, each circle just touching its neighbours. Beneath the picture, written in Japanese, is a question: if you know the size of the big circle, how big are the small ones?
Sometimes the answer is written underneath. Sometimes it isn't.

These boards are called sangaku. Say "SAHN-gah-koo." It means "mathematics tablet." For more than two hundred years, from the 1680s to the late 1800s, people in Japan made them and hung them in shrines and temples.
Why hang a geometry problem in a shrine?
Partly as a gift, or a thank-you, the way people hung other kinds of painted boards. Partly to show off. A sangaku said: here is a problem I solved, and it is beautiful. Can you solve it?
The people who made them were not all scholars. Some were samurai. Some were farmers or merchants. Some were women. Some were children, one as young as twelve.

For most of those years, Japan's rulers kept the country almost closed to the outside world. Japanese mathematicians worked on their own, with their own methods, and they did not know what mathematicians in Europe were doing. Sometimes they found the same things.

One tablet, hung in 1822, shows a ring of six balls, each touching its neighbours, all packed around three other balls. It gives a surprising rule about their sizes. In 1937, an English chemist named Frederick Soddy found the same arrangement, and it was named after him. He did not know about the tablet.
Many sangaku have been lost to fire, rot and time. About nine hundred survive.
Some are still hanging where they were first put up.

events.label: Jantar Mantar at Jaipur

place.name: Jaipur, India (26.92 N, 75.82 E)

events.summary: About 1734. In Jaipur, India, Maharaja Jai Singh II finished an observatory of giant stone instruments for measuring the sky. Its largest sundial is as tall as a nine-storey building.

paragraphs: A stone staircase climbs into the sky. It is as tall as a nine-storey building, and it leads nowhere. On either side of it are huge curved walls, like the inside of a bowl cut in half.
It is a clock.

The staircase is the pointer of a sundial. Its shadow falls on the curved walls, which are marked with the hours and minutes. Because the sundial is so big, its shadow moves fast. Stand beside it and you can watch the edge of the shadow creep along the stone, about a millimetre every second.

The sundial is called the Samrat Yantra, the supreme instrument. It is the largest of about twenty stone instruments in a courtyard in the city of Jaipur, in northwest India. They were built by Maharaja Jai Singh II, who ruled Jaipur and loved astronomy. He finished this observatory around 1734. He built four others in other cities, including Delhi.
Why build instruments so big?

Because he wanted his measurements to be exact. On a small sundial, a minute is a tiny step of shadow, hard to read. On the Samrat Yantra, a minute is about six centimetres. It can tell the local time to within a couple of seconds.

The other instruments measure other things: how high a star is above the horizon, which constellation the Sun is in, where the planets are. Some are bowls sunk into the ground that you climb down into.
Jai Singh knew about telescopes, which had been invented in Europe more than a hundred years before. He chose stone instead. Stone does not bend or wobble, and it lasts.
The name Jantar Mantar comes from Sanskrit words meaning "instrument" and "calculation."
On a sunny day, the Samrat Yantra still tells the time.

events.label: Tupaia's map
events.summary: 1769. On Tahiti, a Polynesian navigator named Tupaia joined Captain Cook's ship and drew a chart of more than seventy islands. Europeans could not read it properly for over two hundred years.

paragraphs: On a sheet of paper, islands are scattered across an empty sea. There are about seventy of them. Their names are written in Tahitian. At the centre is Tahiti.
The man who knew these islands was named Tupaia.

He was born on the island of Raiatea, near Tahiti. He was a priest and a navigator, trained in the knowledge of the sea: how to find your way by the stars, the swells, the winds and the birds. He was descended from the people who first sailed into the Pacific, thousands of years before.

In 1769, the English ship Endeavour, under Captain James Cook, came to Tahiti. When it left, Tupaia went with it. He helped the English talk to the people of the islands. In New Zealand, he could speak with the Māori, whose language is close to Tahitian.
While he was on board, he drew his map, and the ship's officers copied it.
What was strange about it?

The islands were in roughly the right places, but not quite. Some seemed to be in the wrong direction altogether. For more than two hundred years, people who studied the chart thought Tupaia had made mistakes, or that the English had copied it wrong.

In 2019, two researchers suggested another reading, though not everyone agrees. Tupaia had not drawn the ocean from above, as a European chart does. He had drawn it the way a navigator thinks: each island placed by the direction you would sail to reach it, from wherever you were starting. Read that way, the chart makes sense.
Tupaia never came home. He died of illness in 1770, in Batavia, now Jakarta, on the way to England.
The copy made on the ship is in the British Library. If the new reading is right, the islands on it cover a stretch of ocean wider than Australia.

events.label: Haiti becomes free

place.name: Gonaïves, Haiti, where independence was declared (19.45 N, 72.69 W)

events.summary: 1 January 1804. After thirteen years of war, people who had been enslaved in the French colony of Saint-Domingue declared it the free country of Haiti. It was the first country founded by an uprising of enslaved people.

paragraphs: In 1789, the French colony of Saint-Domingue, in the Caribbean, was the richest colony in the world. It grew about four tenths of the world's sugar and more than half of Europe's coffee.
About half a million of the people there were enslaved.

They had been brought from Africa in chains, or were the children of people who had. They worked on sugar plantations, where the work was so hard that many died within a few years of arriving. About thirty thousand French colonists, and some free people of colour, owned the land.
In August 1791, the enslaved people rose up. Plantations burned. The war that followed lasted thirteen years, and at times the armies of France, Spain and Britain were all fighting there.

A formerly enslaved man named Toussaint Louverture became the leader. Say "too-SAN loo-ver-TOOR." In 1794, France ended slavery in all its colonies. But in 1802, Napoleon, who now ruled France, sent an army to take the colony back and bring slavery back with it. Toussaint was captured and taken to a cold prison in the mountains of France, where he died.

The war went on without him. The French army was beaten, by the fighting and by yellow fever. On 1 January 1804, the new leader, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, declared the country independent and gave it the name its first people had used: Haiti.
What did it cost?

Nobody knows the full number. Tens of thousands of French soldiers died. Many more Haitians died, perhaps a hundred thousand or more, and in 1804 Dessalines ordered the killing of most of the French who remained. The plantations were ruined.
In 1825, France demanded that Haiti pay for the plantations it had lost, as the price of being recognised. Haiti was paying it off, with interest, until 1947.

events.label: Suez Canal opens

place.name: Ismailia, midway along the canal, Egypt (30.60 N, 32.27 E)

events.summary: 17 November 1869. The Suez Canal opened in Egypt, joining the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. Ships between Europe and Asia no longer had to sail around Africa.

paragraphs: Look at a map of Africa and Asia. At the top right corner of Africa, a narrow strip of desert joins it to Asia. On one side is the Mediterranean Sea. On the other is the Red Sea, which leads to the Indian Ocean.
For thousands of years, that strip of sand was in the way.
A ship sailing from London to India had to go all the way around Africa. If you could cut through the strip, the journey would be about seven thousand kilometres shorter.

People had tried before. Egyptian kings, thousands of years ago, dug canals from the Nile to the Red Sea, and those canals filled with sand again. In the 1850s, a French diplomat named Ferdinand de Lesseps got permission from Egypt's ruler to try again, and to cut straight across the desert.
Digging began in 1859. It took ten years.
Who dug it?

For the first years, most of the work was done by Egyptian peasants, forced to leave their villages and dig. Tens of thousands worked at a time, many with nothing but picks and baskets, in the heat, often short of water. Thousands died, of heat, thirst and disease. Nobody knows how many.
In 1864, forced labour on the canal was stopped. After that, most of the digging was done by huge steam machines, some of them designed for the job.
The canal opened on 17 November 1869, with a procession of ships and a party for kings and queens from Europe. It was 164 kilometres long. It has been widened and deepened many times since.
Egypt had paid a large part of the cost. Within a few years, it was so deep in debt that it had to sell its share of the canal to Britain.
The canal has no locks. The two seas are at almost the same height, so the water lies nearly still.

events.label: Krakatoa explodes

place.name: Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, Indonesia (6.10 S, 105.42 E)

events.summary: 27 August 1883. The volcanic island of Krakatoa, in what is now Indonesia, blew apart. It made the loudest sound in recorded history, heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away.

paragraphs: On Rodrigues, a small island in the Indian Ocean, the chief of police heard what sounded like the roar of heavy guns, far away to the east. He thought a ship was in trouble.
It was a volcano, nearly five thousand kilometres away.

The volcano was Krakatoa, an island between Java and Sumatra, in what is now Indonesia. It had been rumbling for months. On the morning of 27 August 1883, it blew itself apart in a series of explosions. The biggest came just after ten o'clock.
Is that really the loudest sound ever?

It is the loudest in recorded history. At 160 kilometres away, it was louder than a rock concert heard from the front row. Sailors on a ship about 60 kilometres away wrote that half the crew's eardrums had burst.

Sound is a wave of pressure moving through the air. Most of the Krakatoa wave was too low to hear, but instruments caught it. In cities around the world, weather instruments that measure air pressure showed a jump as the wave passed. Then another jump, hours later, as the wave came back the other way. Some instruments saw it pass seven times, as it went back and forth around the Earth for five days.
The explosions also pushed up huge waves in the sea, which ran up onto the coasts of Java and Sumatra. About 36,000 people died, most of them drowned.
Ash and a fine mist from the eruption spread around the world. For months, sunsets were strangely red. In New York that November, the sky glowed so red that people called out fire engines.
Most of the island was gone. In 1927, a new island rose out of the sea where it had been. It is called Anak Krakatau, "child of Krakatoa," and it is still erupting.

events.label: Tunguska explosion

place.name: near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River, Siberia, Russia (60.89 N, 101.89 E)

events.summary: 30 June 1908. Over a forest in Siberia, something from space exploded in the air. It flattened millions of trees. No crater has ever been found.

paragraphs: At a trading post in the Siberian forest, early on a summer morning, a man was sitting on the porch. Suddenly the sky to the north seemed to split in two, and fire appeared over the forest. He felt heat so strong that his shirt seemed to be burning. Then a blast threw him off the porch.
The explosion was about sixty kilometres away.

It happened on 30 June 1908, over a forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia. Almost no one lived there. The blast flattened millions of trees across an area bigger than a large city, all lying with their tops pointing away from the middle. At the very middle, strangely, trees were left standing, stripped of their branches, like telegraph poles.
Nobody reached the place for nineteen years.

In 1927, a scientist named Leonid Kulik led an expedition into the forest. He expected to find a crater and a huge meteorite. He found the flattened trees, and the standing poles at the centre. He found no crater. He searched for years and never found the meteorite either.
So what was it?

Most scientists now think it was a piece of rock, or perhaps part of a comet, a few tens of metres across. It came in from space at tremendous speed. The air in front of it pushed back so hard that it heated up and burst apart several kilometres above the ground, before it could hit. The blast did the damage. Almost nothing was left to land.
For a few nights afterwards, the sky over Europe glowed so bright that people in London could read a newspaper outdoors at midnight.
Nobody has ever found a piece of it large enough to be sure.
